claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous grain structure.
The starting alloy combines good plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.
Minimal lattice distortion governs the low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The constituent atoms have nearly equal atomic sizes.
The small atomic-size mismatch produces insufficient solid-solution hardening.
Insufficient solid-solution hardening permits facile dislocation glide.
Deformation in the starting alloy is predominantly grain-boundary-mediated, including facile grain-boundary sliding.
Facile dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding limit strain hardening and reduce yield strength.
The controlled intervention is to substitute approximately 4–5 at% additional Cr for an unspecified base element.
The Cr modification will increase lattice distortion.
The Cr modification may promote limited precipitation of a secondary phase such as a Laves phase.
Increased lattice distortion or secondary-phase precipitates will create additional barriers to dislocation motion.
Increased lattice distortion or secondary-phase precipitates will inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
The Cr-modified alloy will have at least approximately 10% higher hardness than the starting alloy.
The Cr-modified alloy will have at least approximately 10% higher yield strength than the starting alloy.
Cr modification will shift deformation from predominantly grain-boundary-controlled behavior toward behavior involving more dislocation pinning.
The proposed comparison uses identically processed base and Cr-modified alloys tested by nanoindentation and uniaxial compression at room temperature and moderate strain.
The hypothesis is restricted to bulk material at room temperature and moderate strain rates and excludes high-temperature or very-high-strain-rate loading.
